body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Completeness of written asthma action plans at discharge and 90-day emergency revisits in children: a provincial cohort","authors":"Achterberg-Mensah L, Delacroix-Oyelowo T, Brandvold-Ng S","year":2022,"venue":"Journal of Paediatric Respiratory Care","doi":"10.5555/jprc.2022.0317","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We followed 2,340 children aged 2 to 17 discharged after an asthma admission from four hospitals and linked them to provincial emergency department data for 90 days. Plans were scored complete when all five template sections were filled, which happened at 52 percent of discharges. After adjustment for age, prior admissions, admission severity and controller prescription, a complete plan was associated with fewer emergency revisits within 90 days (adjusted hazard ratio 0.72, 95 percent CI 0.58 to 0.89). The association was weaker in children with a previous intensive care admission. Revisits to hospitals other than the discharging hospital made up a fifth of all events. Residual confounding by family engagement cannot be excluded, because families who keep appointments may also receive more complete plans."},{"title":"Raising action plan completeness on a paediatric ward: a before-and-after improvement report","authors":"Quist-Obeng R, Halvorsen-Tan M","year":2019,"venue":"Child Health Improvement Notes","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"On one 28-bed paediatric ward, a nurse-led discharge checklist and weekly feedback raised the proportion of complete asthma action plans from 48 percent to 86 percent over nine months. Emergency revisits within 30 days were 11 percent before and 9 percent after the change, a difference the authors describe as compatible with chance given 210 and 196 discharges in the two periods. Completion fell to 71 percent in the three months after feedback stopped. Parents reported that the yellow-zone section was the part most often explained in a hurry at discharge. The report did not adjust for season or for changes in controller prescribing over the same period."},{"title":"Written action plans for children with asthma: a systematic review of effects on urgent care use","authors":"Rasmussen-Adu K, Petrov-Lindqvist E, Okafor-Grey J, Sato-Mbeki H","year":2020,"venue":"Paediatric Evidence Reviews","doi":"10.5555/per.2020.0412","providerType":"review","abstract":"We searched four databases to 2019 for trials and controlled studies of written asthma action plans in children. Twelve studies with 3,105 children met the inclusion criteria. In seven randomised trials, action plans reduced urgent care visits (risk ratio 0.78, 95 percent CI 0.64 to 0.95), with substantial heterogeneity between trials. Plans based on symptoms and plans based on peak flow performed similarly. No study examined how complete the plans were, and only two measured whether families still had the plan at follow-up. Most trials delivered plans together with structured education, so the effect of the written plan alone is uncertain."},{"title":"Measuring the completeness of paediatric asthma action plans: development and reliability of a five-item score","authors":"Mwangi-Laurent A, Oduya-Fischer P, Castellanos-Webb D","year":2021,"venue":"Journal of Paediatric Respiratory Care","doi":"10.5555/jprc.2021.0098","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We developed a five-item completeness score for paper asthma action plans covering daily medicines, signs of worsening, yellow-zone actions, emergency criteria and a booked follow-up appointment. Two respiratory educators independently scored 240 scanned plans. Agreement was good for the total score (kappa 0.81) and lowest for the yellow-zone item (kappa 0.64), where handwritten doses were often illegible. Only 38 percent of plans scored five of five. Scoring took about two minutes per plan. We recommend treating an illegible dose as missing and reporting item-level completeness alongside the total score."},{"title":"Understanding of asthma action plans among caregivers with limited English proficiency","authors":"Nakashima-Obi Y, Ferreira-Holm C","year":2018,"venue":"Family Health Literacy Quarterly","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We assessed 152 caregivers of children discharged after an asthma admission, using a teach-back task on the yellow zone of the family's own plan. Caregivers who preferred a language other than English described the correct yellow-zone steps in 44 percent of cases, compared with 79 percent of English-preferring caregivers. Plans had been written in English for all families, and an interpreter had been used at discharge for 21 of 58 families who needed one. Caregivers with lower health literacy scores were also less accurate. The study was done at one children's hospital and did not follow children for later emergency visits."},{"title":"Where do children go after an asthma discharge? Emergency revisits outside the discharging hospital","authors":"Brennan-Achebe S, Varga-Oduya L","year":2024,"venue":"Northern Child Health Services Review","doi":"10.5555/nchsr.2024.0056","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Using provincial emergency department data, we followed 3,880 children discharged after an asthma admission from two children's hospitals. Within 90 days, 17 percent had at least one asthma-related emergency visit. Of these revisits, 21 percent took place at a hospital other than the discharging one, most often a community hospital closer to home. Children from the lowest neighbourhood income quintile were more likely to revisit elsewhere. Studies that count only revisits to the discharging hospital would miss about one revisit in five and would under-count revisits most among lower-income families, biasing comparisons that differ by income."},{"title":"Confounding by severity in observational studies of asthma discharge interventions","authors":"Lindqvist-Oyelaran M, Adeyemi-Holt B, Tanaka-Reid F","year":2016,"venue":"Methods in Child Health Research","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We examined 14 observational studies of discharge interventions for childhood asthma, including action plans, education sessions and follow-up calls. In 11 studies, children who received the intervention differed from those who did not in markers of severity or family engagement, most often previous admissions and controller use. Only four studies adjusted for a measure of prior health care use, and none used an active comparator or a negative control outcome. We describe a minimum adjustment set (age, previous admissions in 12 months, admission severity, controller at discharge and area income) and recommend a negative control outcome such as injury visits."}]}
